headline: Proposed ordinance would ban Flock license plate cameras, with more talks planned before any vote.
summary: Councilor Govan's ordinance would ban automatic license plate readers (ALPRs), including Flock cameras, for any city entity. It would also bar the city from getting such data from other entities and seek to wind down existing contracts. The committee will meet with the law department first, then hold a follow-up meeting before the ordinance goes to the council floor.
discussion: Outside searches of city data: Public speakers said agencies outside the city searched Springfield's Flock data about 9 million times between January 2024 and early December 2025. Police said they restricted searches to agencies they believed were better suited to share with, around late January or early February.

Ordinance scope: The city's associate solicitor said the ordinance as drafted would ban ALPRs, block city access to data from other entities, and wind down existing contracts. Council members asked whether to regulate use instead, and whether the ordinance should include emergency exceptions.

Privacy and data concerns: Public speakers raised worries about stalking, targeting of immigrants, and how long images are kept. Flock's public affairs manager said the company does not sell data and deletes images after 30 days.
Police defense of the cameras: Police said the cameras help solve violent crimes and find missing vehicles. They cited a stolen car with a 7-month-old baby inside that was located quickly.
